html:
Ramkhamhaeng was the third king of Sukhothai, an early Thai kingdom in what is now north central Thailand, ruling from about 1279 to 1298. Thais honour him as a founder of the nation; see Sukhothai and Ayutthaya.

Under him Sukhothai reached its widest sway, with lords from Laos to the Malay peninsula paying respect. He sent missions to the Yuan court in China. He supported Theravada Buddhism, bringing monks from Nakhon Si Thammarat in the south.

He is credited with creating the Thai script in 1283, adapted from Khmer writing. The source for this, and for much of what is known about him, is the Ram Khamhaeng Inscription, a stone found in 1833 by the future King Mongkut, then a monk. It describes a fair ruler who hung a bell at his gate so that any subject could ring it and ask for justice, and a land where "there is fish in the water and rice in the fields". Some scholars have argued the stone was made much later, but most accept it as old.
